questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Tests basic understanding of Kubernetes security posture and practical gate design in CI, covering both Pod security and NetworkPolicy defaults.

## Key Concepts
- Pod securityContext and container.securityContext
- Kyverno vs OPA Gatekeeper for policy enforcement
- Default-deny NetworkPolicy per Namespace
- Local validation with kubectl and kyverno/opa tooling
- CI validation with GitHub Actions hooks

## Code Example
```yaml
# Kyverno ClusterPolicy (minimal)
apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata:
  name: require-secctx
spec:
  validationFailureAction: enforce
  rules:
  - name: check-security-context
    match:
      resources:
        kinds: ["Pod"]
    validate:
      message: "Containers must set readOnlyRootFilesystem: true and runAsNonRoot: true"
      pattern:
        spec:
          containers:
          - securityContext:
              readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
              runAsNonRoot: true
              allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
```

```yaml
# NetworkPolicy default-deny (Namespace scope)
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: default-deny
  namespace: example
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes:
  - Ingress
  - Egress
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you adapt the policy to exclude specific namespaces or namespaces with legacy workloads?
- How would you test this in a multi-tenant CI environment with limited cluster access?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Tests understanding of identity-based runtime access control in Kubernetes, integrating SPIRE, OPA Gatekeeper, and admission/mutating webhooks for auditing. It also evaluates plan for cross-cloud (Snowflake/IBM) data workloads and secure Spark job execution.

## Key Concepts
- SPIRE workload identity and attestation
- OPA Gatekeeper constraint templates and validation hooks
- Kubernetes RBAC and API access control
- Mutating webhook for audit sidecars
- Validation strategy with compliant vs noncompliant pods

## Code Example
```yaml
# ConstraintTemplate (example): OPA-based API access gate
apiVersion: templates.gatekeeper.sh/v1beta1
kind: ConstraintTemplate
metadata:
  name: k8sapiaiaccess
spec:
  crd:
    spec:
      names:
        kind: K8sAPIAccess
  targets:
  - target: admission.k8s.gatekeeper.sh
    rego: |-
      package k8sapiaiaccess
      violate["API access denied: identity not whitelisted"] {
        input.review.kind.kind == "Pod"
        identity := input.review.object.metadata.annotations["spire.identity"]
        not identity_in_allowlist(identity)
      }
      
      # allowlisted identities (simplified)
      identity_in_allowlist(id) {
        id == "spiffe://cluster.local/ns/default/sa/spark-sa"
      }
```

```yaml
# Compliant Pod (SPIRE-identity annotated)
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: compliant-spark
  annotations:
    spire.identity: "spiffe://cluster.local/ns/default/sa/spark-sa"
spec:
  serviceAccountName: spark-sa
  containers:
  - name: spark
    image: myrepo/spark:latest
```

```yaml
# Noncompliant Pod (no SPIRE identity)
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: noncompliant-spark
spec:
  containers:
  - name: spark
    image: myrepo/spark:latest
```

## Validation Plan
- Deploy constraint template and constraint; attempt compliant pod deployment; verify admission allows and audit sidecar is injected. 
- Deploy noncompliant pod; confirm admission denies with clear event reason. 
- Run a Spark job and inspect API calls logged by the auditing sidecar for traceability.

deny["envoy-proxy sidecar required"] {
  input.review.object.metadata.labels["data-tier"] == "confidential"

}

has_sidecar(containers, name) {

## Why This Is Asked
Tests practical policy-as-code skills and integration of admission controls into CI for a multi-cloud, large-scale platform.

- Gatekeeper/OPA ConstraintTemplate
- securityContext runAsNonRoot and runAsUser
- privileged and capabilities.drop
- hostPath/hostIPC/hostPID prohibition

## Code Example
```yaml
# ConstraintTemplate (high-level sketch)
apiVersion: templates.gatekeeper.sh/v1beta1
kind: ConstraintTemplate
metadata:
  name: k8sprivilege
spec:
  crd:
    spec:
      names:
        kind: K8sPrivilege
  targets:
  - target: AdmissionReview
    rego: |
      package k8sprivilege
      violation["privilege violation"] {
        input.review.object.kind == "Deployment"
      }
```
```yaml
# Failing manifest (hostPath & privileged)
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: bad-service
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: app
          image: example/app:latest
          securityContext:
            privileged: true
            runAsNonRoot: false
            runAsUser: 0
            capabilities:
              drop: []
      volumes:
        - name: data
          hostPath:
            path: /tmp
            type: Directory
```
```yaml
# Passing manifest (non-root, restricted caps, no hostPath)
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: good-service
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      securityContext:
        runAsNonRoot: true
      containers:
        - name: app
          image: example/app:latest
          securityContext:
            runAsNonRoot: true
            runAsUser: 1000
            privileged: false
            capabilities:
              drop:
                - ALL
      volumes: []
```

- Run Gatekeeper in CI and verify failing/passing manifests via kubectl apply --dry-run and gatekeeper playbooks.
- Confirm PRs fail on bad manifests and pass on good manifests.

```yaml

apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: tenant-a-web-egress
  namespace: tenant-a
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web
  policyTypes:
  - Egress
  egress:
  - to:
    - podSelector: {}
  - to:
    - ipBlock:

    ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 443
  - to:
    - ipBlock:
        cidr: 10.0.0.0/16
    ports:
    - protocol: UDP
      port: 53
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 53
```

package kernel.authz

violation[{"msg": msg}] {
